\chapter{Animals in the Yard}
\label{ch:hi-animals-in-the-yard}
\hlchaptermodality{60}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can name five more animals when I greet the house that keeps them.}

Complete HI-C60-peacock and say all five words in order.

\section[bandar]{\hi{बंदर} (bandar) — a monkey}

\label{lesson:HI-C60-monkey}



\begin{quote}
Before the new run of words: which letter did the piece before this one give you, and where does the tongue go for it?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \hi{बंदर}}
\textbf{\hi{बंदर}} (\emph{bandar}) — \textquotedblleft{}a monkey\textquotedblright{}.

From Sanskrit \hi{वानर} (\emph{vānara}), 'monkey', a word many readers of Sanskrit connect with \hi{वन} (\emph{vana}), 'forest' — the one who belongs to the woods. Prakrit wore it down and a nasal crept in at the front, and \hi{बंदर} came out the other end.

Keep one thing straight before you travel. Persian has its own \emph{bandar}, spelt the same in our letters, and it means a harbour — it is the \emph{bandar} inside a dozen port names on the Indian Ocean. Two different words that happen to sound alike, not one word with two jobs.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
The first of five animals.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{bandar}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{bandar}, then \emph{ghoṛā}, and say which of them a house keeps on purpose
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \hi{बंदर} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a monkey\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[sā̃p]{\hi{साँप} (sā̃p) — a snake}

\label{lesson:HI-C60-snake}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{bandar} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \hi{साँप}}
\textbf{\hi{साँप}} (\emph{sā̃p}) — \textquotedblleft{}a snake\textquotedblright{}.

From Sanskrit \hi{सर्प} (\emph{sarpa}), 'snake', built on \hi{सृप्} (\emph{sṛp-}), 'to creep'. The animal is named for what it does, and Latin did exactly the same thing: \emph{serpēns} is 'the creeping one', from the very same ancient root.

So English \emph{serpent} and Hindi \hi{साँप} are the same word, four thousand years apart, and neither of them borrowed it from the other. The \emph{r} of \hi{सर्प} melted into the \emph{p}, and the nose-vowel you learnt to write is what is left standing where it was.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Two.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{sā̃p}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{sā̃p}, then \emph{bandar}, and say which one you would rather meet
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \hi{साँप} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a snake\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[murgī]{\hi{मुर्गी} (murgī) — a hen}

\label{lesson:HI-C60-hen}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{sā̃p} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \hi{मुर्गी}}
\textbf{\hi{मुर्गी}} (\emph{murgī}) — \textquotedblleft{}a hen\textquotedblright{}.

Persian \ar{مرغ} (\emph{murgh}) meant a bird of any kind, and Hindi narrowed it to the one bird a household actually keeps. \hi{मुर्गा} (\emph{murgā}) is the cock, \hi{मुर्गी} the hen.

This one earns its place at dawn. A \hi{मुर्गा} wakes a village well before any clock does, which is a large part of why nobody in that village ever needed a \hi{घंटा} to do the same job. And note what it is not: \hi{चिड़िया}, which you already own, stays with the small wild birds.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Three.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{murgī}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{murgī}, then \emph{chiṛiyā}, and say which one lives in the yard
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \hi{मुर्गी} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a hen\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[bhaĩs]{\hi{भैंस} (bhaĩs) — a buffalo}

\label{lesson:HI-C60-buffalo}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{murgī} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \hi{भैंस}}
\textbf{\hi{भैंस}} (\emph{bhaĩs}) — \textquotedblleft{}a buffalo\textquotedblright{}.

From Sanskrit \hi{महिषी} (\emph{mahiṣī}), the female of \hi{महिष} (\emph{mahiṣa}), 'buffalo'. The feminine is the form that survived into everyday Hindi, because the female is the animal a household has reason to talk about every day.

Most of the milk in North India comes from a \hi{भैंस} and not from a \hi{गाय}, which is the opposite of what an English speaker expects. \hi{दूध} and the sweets built on it all start here.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Four.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{bhaĩs}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{bhaĩs}, then \emph{gāy}, and say which one fills the \hi{दूध} pail
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \hi{भैंस} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a buffalo\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[mor]{\hi{मोर} (mor) — a peacock}

\label{lesson:HI-C60-peacock}



\begin{quote}
Name the 4 words of this chapter so far.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \hi{मोर}}
\textbf{\hi{मोर}} (\emph{mor}) — \textquotedblleft{}a peacock\textquotedblright{}.

From Sanskrit \hi{मयूर} (\emph{mayūra}). The \emph{y} dropped out, the two vowels ran together, and a three-piece word became a one-piece one — the same wearing-down you have watched happen to a dozen words by now.

\hi{मयूर} itself is still alive in formal Hindi and in names, so the two forms sit side by side: the old one on a wedding card, \hi{मोर} in the yard. And the yard is where you meet it — a \hi{मोर} walks into a village at dusk the way a pigeon walks into a city square.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Five: \hi{बंदर}, \hi{साँप}, \hi{मुर्गी}, \hi{भैंस}, \hi{मोर}. Enough to name what lives around a house you are greeting.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{mor}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item all five in order, then \emph{namaste} to whoever keeps them
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \hi{मोर} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a peacock\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
